blocks.title: What appears here, and what does not
text: A paper is published on this site only if RCF English created it, the copyright holder has given permission for it to be distributed, it has been personally approved for publication, or it can lawfully be **linked** from the official website that publishes it.

A paper is never published merely because a copy of it exists somewhere. This means the collection here grows more slowly than some others — deliberately. Read the [Copyright and Resource Policy](copyright-policy/).

blocks.title: What the “Clear scan” label means
text: The papers above carry a **Clear scan** label. It is given only after a person has opened the PDF and looked at the first page on screen, and seen that it is straight, sharp, complete, printed rather than handwritten, and carries **no student name**.

It is not awarded because the text copies out neatly. That test proved misleading: two Grade 10 papers read perfectly as text, yet one is visibly tilted and the other has *Teacher Copy* written across it by hand. Both are still in the collection, and neither carries the label.
Every other paper on the site is still worth using. It simply has not been through that check yet.

blocks.title: What this collection actually contains
text: **The papers are heavily weighted to 2019.** That is the shape of the collection, not a gap in the filtering. Most of the papers gathered so far come from 2018 and 2019, and **there are no 2023 papers at all**. A few recent papers are included, and they are generally the clearest scans.
**The files are not stored on this website.** Each paper opens in Google Drive. *View the paper* reads it in your browser; *Download PDF* saves it. Nothing is copied onto this site.
**More papers are still being checked.** A paper is added only after somebody has opened the file and confirmed what is in it, so this list grows slowly and will keep growing.

pages.title: How to Use Past Papers
pages.description: How to get real value from past papers: when to start, how to work under timed conditions, how to mark your own script, and the mistake almost every student makes.
pages.keywords: how to use past papers, timed practice, self marking, revision method

hero.text: Most students do past papers wrongly: too late, untimed, and without marking them. All three faults are easy to correct.

blocks.heading: The mistake almost everyone makes
text: Past papers are kept for the last month, worked through quickly, and never marked. The student finishes with a vague sense of having "done papers" and no idea what went wrong.
A past paper is not a test. It is a **teaching instrument**, and the teaching happens after you put the pen down.

blocks.heading: How to use one paper properly
intro: This takes about three hours in total for a full paper. Three papers used this way are worth more than fifteen worked through carelessly.

items.title: Work it under real conditions
text: By hand, to time, in one sitting, without notes and without your telephone. Anything else measures something other than what the examination measures.

items.title: Stop when the time stops
text: Draw a line where you were when the time ran out, then, if you wish, continue in a different colour. The line tells you the truth about your timing, which is information you badly need.

items.title: Leave it for a day
text: You cannot see your own errors an hour after writing. A day's gap makes you a much better marker of your own work.

items.title: Mark it yourself, with the guidance beside you
text: Use a marking scheme if one is lawfully available, or the checklists in the lessons on this site. Give yourself a mark, honestly. Being generous to yourself now is expensive later.

items.title: Write down your three biggest losses
text: Not every error — the three that cost the most marks. *Ran out of time on the essay. Wrote a notice without a date. Answered only half of question 4.*

items.title: Rewrite one answer properly
text: Only one. The weakest one. This single step is where nearly all the improvement happens, and it is the step almost everybody skips.

blocks.heading: When to start
text: **Earlier than you think.** Not in the last month — from the point at which you have covered a task type.
Learnt how a notice is laid out? Do the notice question from three papers this week. That is fifteen minutes' work and it makes the learning permanent.
Save complete, timed papers for the last two months. Use individual questions from the beginning.

blocks.heading: A term-by-term plan
columns: What to do with past papers
rows: Single questions on task types you have just studied. Untimed at first, then timed.
Half papers, timed. Mark them yourself. Begin keeping a list of your recurring errors.
One complete paper a fortnight, under full conditions. Mark, note three losses, rewrite one answer.
One complete paper a week. Revise your own marked scripts, not new material.
No new papers. Reread your own error list and your best answers. Sleep.

blocks.heading: Marking your own script honestly
text: Self-marking is a skill, and it can be learnt. Ask these questions of each answer in turn.
bullets: **Did I answer the question that was asked**, or one close to it?
**Did I answer every part** of a multi-part question?
**Is the form correct** — notice, email, letter, essay, speech?
**Is the length appropriate** to the marks?
**Would someone else understand my handwriting** here?
**How many marks did I lose to errors I could have caught** in the last ten minutes?
**Where exactly did I run out of time?** — this is usually the largest single loss on the paper.

blocks.title: About model answers
text: When you compare your answer with a model, you are not looking for the same words. You are looking for the same **structure**.

Model answers on this site are teaching material written by RCF English. They are not official answers and they are not the only acceptable ones. Do not memorise them — a memorised answer will not fit the question you are actually asked.

blocks.title: Prescribed texts change between years
text: A past Literature paper may be set on texts that are no longer prescribed. The **questions** remain useful — they show you the kinds of question asked and how they are worded — even when the texts differ. Check the current official syllabus for your own year.

hero.text: Papers for Advanced Level English Literature. Unseen appreciation questions from any year are useful, whatever the prescribed texts were.

blocks.title: Old papers are still useful — for two things
bullets: **Unseen appreciation questions never expire.** A poem or passage set ten years ago is exactly as useful for practice as one set last year, because nothing was prescribed.

**Question wording is stable even when texts change.** Reading twenty essay questions on texts you have not studied teaches you how such questions are constructed — which is precisely what you need in order to read your own question properly.

blocks.title: What a model paper is
text: A model paper is written to resemble the examination in structure, in the kinds of question asked and in the time it takes. It is **not** an official paper and is not set by any examination authority.
Model papers published here are written by RCF English, or are published with the permission of whoever wrote them. The source is shown against each one.

hero.text: A full paper takes three hours and a whole afternoon to use properly. A revision paper takes thirty minutes, which means you will actually do it.

blocks.title: Why short papers are often more useful
text: A complete paper is the right instrument in the last two months. Before that it is usually the wrong one: it takes too long, it mixes too many skills together, and the feedback arrives too late to be acted on.
A revision paper on one task — notices, or context questions, or tenses — can be attempted, marked and learnt from in under an hour. Six of those in a term will teach more than two complete papers.

hero.text: A marking scheme is the most useful document in revision — and the most misused.

blocks.title: Marking schemes and copyright
text: An official marking scheme belongs to the body that produced it. RCF English publishes one only where the copyright holder has given permission, and otherwise links to the official source where the official source publishes it.
Marking **guidance** written by RCF English is original material and is published freely. It is clearly distinguished from any official scheme.

blocks.heading: How to use a marking scheme
numbered: **Write the answer first.** A marking scheme read before the attempt teaches nothing, because you cannot then see what you would have done.
**Mark against it honestly.** Being generous to yourself is the commonest self-marking error and the most expensive.

**Look at what it rewards, not only at the answers.** A scheme tells you what examiners are looking for — content points, structure, accuracy, appropriateness — and that information transfers to every other question.
**Do not memorise scheme answers.** They are answers to that question, not templates.
**Notice where marks are cheap.** Most schemes contain marks for things like correct form and complete answers, which cost nothing but attention.
